sections.text:
We consider a task planning scenario in which robots sharing a persistent environment are assigned tasks one at a time from a held-out sequence.

Standard task planners, lacking foresight of future tasks and inconsiderate of others' constraints, solve each task in isolation, leaving terminal states that increase future cost for all; side effects that compound over lengthy task sequences.

To reduce cost over the sequence, a robot must anticipate how its actions now may impact performance on future tasks for all robots sharing the environment.

Therefore, we present courteous anticipatory planning, wherein a model-based planner proposes candidate plans and selects the one that jointly minimizes immediate cost and aggregated expected future cost across all robots, estimated via independent per-robot learned estimators.

This factored formulation avoids combinatorial joint rollouts and supports modular deployment: adding a robot requires only training its own estimator.

We evaluate in two persistent PDDL domains, a home environment with robots that have similar capabilities but different responsibilities, and a restaurant environment where robots' distinct capabilities create states that other robots lack the capability to resolve.

During lengthy task sequences, our planner reduces total cost by 10.4% versus myopic and 4.5% versus selfish anticipatory planning in a two-robot home environment and by 20.5% and 6.7%, respectively, in a three-robot restaurant.

items.title: Courteous Anticipation: Improving Long-Lived Task Planning in Persistent Shared Environments

sections.text:
For robots to assist, serve, and collaborate with humans, they must not only interpret human requests conveyed through language and multimodal intentional cues, but also execute long-horizon tasks that interleave navigation and manipulation. In this paper, we introduce HEIR, a resource for studying how to Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interaction.

HEIR pairs human speech, measured gaze, and egocentric video with robot observations and teleoperated navigation-manipulation trajectories, while each session preserves successive episodes, with each request fulfilled through multiple execution subtasks.

The captured data, together with human-authored annotations, support the study of intent grounding, execution planning, and task completion within a unified interaction setting.

To demonstrate the value of HEIR, we conduct extensive offline experiments to evaluate how models benefit from additional human-centric context across these tasks, together with real-robot experiments that assess execution task completion.

HEIR thus provides a valuable resource for studying user-centric robot interaction in naturalistic household environments. Our demo and dataset are available online.

items.title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions

sections.text:
Collaborative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate with a partially observed partner while physically interacting through shared objects. This is difficult because failures often arise not from poor local skills, but from mistimed waiting, yielding, pulling, releasing, or repositioning.

We study this problem with two bimanual mobile manipulators coupled through rigid and deformable objects. We propose Sequential Asymmetric Imitation (SAI), a single-teleoperator curriculum for learning coupled multi-robot behaviors without synchronized dual-operator demonstrations or explicit inter-robot communication.

SAI trains Robot A from unilateral demonstrations with a compliant human partner, trains Robot B against the deployed Robot A policy, and then refines Robot A using sparse interventions near coordination failures.

This staged process exposes the policies to increasingly realistic partner behaviors, including delay, phase mismatch,insufficient yielding, and interaction conflict. Across real-world dual-robot manipulation tasks, SAI improves task success, phase synchronization, and partner-contingent yielding over independent imitation and curriculum-ablation baselines.

These results suggest that physically coupled collaboration can be learned through the structure of the imitation curriculum, rather than through synchronized multi-operator demonstrations or explicit coordination mechanisms. More videos on project page:http://cyc0429.github.io/sai-project-page/

sections.text:
The rapid evolution of Embodied AI has enabled Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to excel in multimodal perception and task execution.

However, applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to these massive models in large-scale distributed environments faces severe systemic bottlenecks, primarily due to the resource conflict between high-fidelity physical simulation and the intensive VRAM/bandwidth demands of deep learning.

This conflict often leaves overall throughput constrained by execution-phase inefficiencies. To address these challenges, we propose D-VLA, a high-concurrency, low-latency distributed RL framework for large-scale embodied foundation models.

D-VLA introduces "Plane Decoupling," physically isolating high-frequency training data from low-frequency weight control to eliminate interference between simulation and optimization. We further design a four-thread asynchronous "Swimlane" pipeline, enabling full parallel overlap of sampling, inference, gradient computation, and parameter distribution.

Additionally, a dual-pool VRAM management model and topology-aware replication resolve memory fragmentation and optimize communication efficiency. Experiments on benchmarks like LIBERO show that D-VLA significantly outperforms mainstream RL frameworks in throughput and sampling efficiency for billion-parameter VLA models.

In trillion-parameter scalability tests, our framework maintains exceptional stability and linear speedup, providing a robust system for high-performance general-purpose embodied agents.

summary.en: The paper presents D-VLA, a distributed asynchronous reinforcement learning framework for large embodied foundation models. It separates high-frequency training data from low-frequency weight control and uses a four-thread pipeline to overlap sampling, inference, gradient computation, and parameter distribution. Dual-pool VRAM management and topology-aware replication address memory and communication issues. The authors report higher throughput and sampling efficiency than mainstream RL frameworks on benchmarks including LIBERO, and stable linear speedup in trillion-parameter scalability tests.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向大规模具身基础模型的分布式异步强化学习框架 D-VLA，旨在缓解物理仿真与模型训练之间的资源冲突。框架通过训练数据与权重控制解耦、四线程异步流水线、双池显存管理及拓扑感知复制来提升并行度和通信效率。作者称，在 LIBERO 等基准上，D-VLA 对十亿参数 VLA 模型的吞吐量和采样效率优于主流强化学习框架；万亿参数扩展测试中保持稳定并呈线性加速。

sections.text:
Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis.

In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption.

This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots.

Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications.

Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

summary.en: The paper proposes a friction model for continuum robots interacting with their environment, based on complementarity constraints and the Coulomb friction assumption. The model represents static and sliding friction, motion hysteresis, and interaction-induced robot deformation; the authors state that it can run in real time. Experiments with a 287.9 mm tendon-driven continuum robot showed that including friction reduced maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm with a frictionless model to 5.85 mm.
summary.zh: 论文针对连续体机器人的环境接触摩擦，提出基于库仑摩擦假设和互补约束的模型，可描述静摩擦、滑动摩擦、运动迟滞及相应的机器人变形，并称其可实时实现。实验使用一台长287.9毫米的腱驱动连续体机器人进行验证；与无摩擦模型相比，加入摩擦的模型将末端位置最大误差从45.4毫米降至5.85毫米。

sections.text:
Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates.

Existing transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy.

We introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack unchanged.

Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift by nearly a factor of six.

summary.en: The paper introduces a body-aligned virtual joint space before the existing transmission mapping. Policy actions and observations use a shared anatomical convention, while a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to each robot’s native coordinates without changing the transmission or low-level control stack. The authors report that, under one unchanged training recipe, this interface tracks accurately, aligns the feet with travel direction, and trains stably on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts. On Unitree G1 hardware, heading drift is reduced by nearly a factor of six.
summary.zh: 论文提出在机器人传动映射之前加入身体对齐的虚拟关节空间，使策略的动作和观测遵循共同的解剖约定，再由确定性运动学层映射到各机器人的原生关节坐标，同时保留现有传动与底层控制。作者报告，在三个腿部轴布局不同的人形机器人上使用同一未修改训练方案时，该接口能够准确跟踪、保持足部与行进方向对齐并稳定训练；在 Unitree G1 硬件上，航向漂移接近降低六倍。

sections.text:
When learning probabilistic policies from human demonstrations, data-efficient learning and fast adaptations to new scenarios are key requirements. One popular way to achieve intuitive and reliable adaptations is through non-parametric, typically kernel-based, methods.

However, existing solutions either fail to account for the geometry of manifolds common in robotics, limiting data efficiency, or, when geometry-aware, provide unreliable uncertainty estimates or require retraining to adapt.

We propose a non-parametric approach leveraging geometric priors in scenarios of data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties for probabilistic modeling.

We utilize the method to formulate policies based on time or robot state, where non-separable diagonal kernels allow capturing uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for same-sized in- and outputs. Fast updates, requiring less than 3 ms for a trajectory involving both position and orientation are possible through an optimized formulation.

Our approach supports both manifold-valued input and manifold-valued output with large orientation changes. Using task parameterization, adaptation to different object poses is easily possible. We evaluate the approach on a set of toy examples and on real robot manipulation tasks both in autonomous execution and in shared control scenarios.

summary.en: The paper proposes a non-parametric imitation learning approach that combines geometric priors with heteroscedastic uncertainty for probabilistic policies learned from demonstrations. Non-separable diagonal kernels model uncertainty relationships between input and output degrees of freedom of equal size. The approach supports manifold-valued inputs and outputs, including large orientation changes, and task parameterization enables adaptation to different object poses. The authors report trajectory updates in under 3 ms for position and orientation. Evaluation covers toy examples and real robot manipulation in autonomous execution and shared control.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种结合几何先验与异方差不确定性的非参数模仿学习方法，面向示范数据有限且需要适应新场景的概率策略。该方法使用非可分离对角核建模同维输入与输出自由度之间的不确定性关系，支持流形值输入和输出，包括较大的方向变化；作者称，涉及位置和方向的轨迹更新耗时少于3毫秒。通过任务参数化，策略可适应不同物体位姿。评估包括玩具示例及真实机器人操作任务，涵盖自主执行和共享控制。

sections.text:
Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable.

We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness.

We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use.

We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none.

On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself.

On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%.Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks.

These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

summary.en: The paper trains an open-weight 27B reasoning model to control robots through reinforcement learning conducted entirely in simulation, without demonstrations or a control harness. The authors report transfer to an unseen robot, the real world, and novel instructions. On a real dual-arm robot, the trained model succeeds in 60% of trials, while the base model succeeds in none; LIBERO success rises from 1.6% to 74.4%. On LIBERO-Pro, it succeeds in 57.4% of episodes for new tasks in familiar scenes. The authors report no measurable degradation across nine reasoning, coding, and vision benchmarks.

sections.text:
Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment.

When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution.

However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance.

We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry.

We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition.

Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.

summary.en: The paper proposes a two-stage informative-planning framework for unknown disturbances that vary spatially but remain time-invariant. It first identifies where measurements of quantities of interest are needed, generates alternative paths, and prioritizes disturbance sampling by its expected reduction of uncertainty along those paths. It then incorporates the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0–52.3% compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种面向未知、空间变化但时间不变扰动的两阶段信息规划方法，用于时空环境监测。方法先确定需要测量关注量的位置并生成候选路径，再按扰动测量对路径上扰动不确定性的预期降低程度安排采样优先级；随后将学习到的扰动信念纳入轨迹优化，以考虑扰动对机器人运动和信息获取的影响。四种仿真情境中，该方法相较于全环境扰动估计，将扰动学习时间缩短 25.0%–52.3%，并找到在考虑扰动后更合适、但按名义动力学看代价较高的路径。

sections.text:
A fundamental challenge in robotic teleoperation is enabling an operator to control a remote robot as effortlessly and intuitively as their own hands. Despite the growing use of teleoperation to collect demonstrations for training autonomous robot policies, teleoperated performance still falls significantly short of human dexterity, even for basic tasks.

Here, we present evidence that a key factor contributing to this performance gap is the absence of localized tactile feedback.

We equip a two-degree-of-freedom (DoF) bilateral force-feedback telemanipulator with a vision-based tactile sensor and a 32-pixel tactile display, allowing us to capture spatial contact patterns on the robot finger and render them on the operator's fingertip.

In teleoperated button-discrimination and peg-rolling tasks, we demonstrate that reproducing spatially distributed contact information brings teleoperated movements closer to natural human behavior through fewer unnecessary motions and task completion steps, significantly reducing task completion time and producing more consistent demonstrations across trials and operators.

We further show that these improvements in human demonstrations can propagate to autonomous policies: policies trained on tactile-enhanced demonstrations exhibited similar reductions in both task completion time and deviation from natural human behavior.

Together, these results establish spatially distributed tactile feedback as an important component of dexterous robotic teleoperation and demonstrate its potential to improve safety-critical teleoperation and enable more humanlike demonstrations for training autonomous robot policies.

summary.en: The paper investigates localized tactile feedback in robotic teleoperation. The researchers equip a two-degree-of-freedom bilateral force-feedback telemanipulator with vision-based tactile sensing and a 32-pixel display that renders spatial contact patterns on the operator’s fingertip. In button-discrimination and peg-rolling tasks, the authors report fewer unnecessary motions and task steps, shorter completion times, and more consistent demonstrations across trials and operators. Autonomous policies trained on the tactile-enhanced demonstrations show similar reductions in task time and deviation from natural human behavior. The authors describe spatially distributed tactile feedback as a component of dexterous teleoperation.

sections.text:
Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it.

In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met.

Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed).

We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control.

The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.

summary.en: The paper studies handover robustness after cooperative self-play training in a physics-based parcel-transfer scenario involving a Unitree G1 and a learned giver. The receiver succeeds in 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner across two training seeds, but in only 31% with unfamiliar scripted partners. The authors attribute the gap to the giver always starting immediately under a shared reward, which teaches the receiver a single rendezvous timing. Hidden start-delay randomisation, unobserved by the receiver, raises success with unseen scripted partners to 80% in both seeds after 300 further updates. The authors also report three- to five-fold reductions in high-force contact.
summary.zh: 论文研究人形机器人在自我对弈训练后与陌生伙伴交接物品时的鲁棒性，并指出伙伴开始递交的时机延迟是关键因素。在基于物理的包裹交接中，接收方与训练伙伴的成功率为 95% 和 90%，与未见过的脚本伙伴则为 31%。作者将问题归因于共享奖励下学习到的递交方总是立即开始，导致接收方只学会一种会合时机。加入接收方无法观察到的隐藏开始延迟随机化，经过 300 次进一步更新后，两个训练种子下对陌生脚本伙伴的成功率均升至 80%；高力度接触减少三至五倍。

Legged-wheeled robots have been extensively studied for their potential to combine the efficient flat-ground mobility of wheels with the rough-terrain adaptability of legs. However, their application to long-distance autonomous navigation in real environments remains limited.

This paper reports our efforts to build a deep reinforcement learning-based locomotion controller and an autonomous navigation system for the commercially available Go2-W legged-wheeled robot. The study focuses on the integrated system and the practical challenges associated with its sustained operation over long distances in real-world environments.

For locomotion control, we extended our proprioception-only policy, previously developed for quadruped robots, to Go2-W, a 16-degree-of-freedom legged-wheeled robot. To address this issue, we developed a policy with periodic foot-lifting motion that distributes the joint loads and mitigates heat concentration. We evaluated the integrated system at the Tsukuba Challenge 2025.

summary.en: The paper presents a deep reinforcement learning locomotion controller and autonomous navigation system for the commercial Go2-W legged-wheeled robot, focusing on sustained long-distance operation in real environments. They introduce periodic foot lifting to distribute joint loads. In an evaluation at the Tsukuba Challenge 2025, the robot autonomously traversed an approximately 2.8-kilometer route with sidewalks, a park, and stairs without stopping due to overheating.

sections.text:
Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them.

We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement.

It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors.

Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.

summary.en: The paper introduces ERA, a training-free object navigation system that uses depth predicted from RGB images and poses in place of a depth sensor. The authors argue that treating predicted depth as sensor data can accumulate view-dependent mapping errors, remove exploration goals, and end searches prematurely. ERA uses revisable occupancy mapping, explores from reachable viewpoints when no frontier remains, and checks targets across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors, according to the authors. Under the same predicted depth, its map and exploration components raise VLFM success from 10.8% to 61.7%. The paper also reports a real-robot deployment.
summary.zh: 论文提出 ERA，一种无需训练、以 RGB 图像和位姿预测深度来执行物体导航的系统。作者指出，若把预测深度当作传感器读数建图，视角相关误差会累积，可能消除探索目标并使搜索过早结束。ERA采用可修订占据地图，并从可达视点继续探索，即使当前没有前沿；系统还会跨视角确认目标再停止。在三个基准测试中，作者报告 ERA 在无深度传感器的免训练方法中达到先进表现；相同预测深度下，其地图和探索组件使 VLFM 成功率由 10.8% 升至 61.7%。论文还报告了真实机器人部署。

sections.text:
Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays.

A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous.

Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances.

We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader.

The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels.

This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. Videos: https://sites.google.com/leggedrobotics.com/heavy-metal-acrobatics This is the author's version of the work.

It is posted here by permission of the AAAS for personal use, not for redistribution. The definitive version was published in Science Robotics on 11 November 2026, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aef0894

summary.en: The authors use reinforcement learning in simulation and transfer the learned policies to a 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies make the machine rise onto two wheels and, while balancing, cross rough terrain, follow specified trajectories, spin, and swing its bucket before landing on four wheels. The authors state that these results demonstrate dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery through reinforcement learning and sim-to-real transfer.
summary.zh: 本文研究如何自动控制具有复杂液压动力学、体积大且实验风险高的重型机械。作者在仿真中使用强化学习训练策略，再将其迁移到一台约5吨的滑移装载机上。该策略可使机器摆上两轮，并在两轮平衡时越过崎岖地形、沿指定轨迹行驶、旋转及摆动铲斗，最后安全落回四轮。作者据此声称，强化学习与仿真到现实迁移可实现重型机械的动态自主控制。

items.title: Heavy Metal Acrobatics: Learning Dynamic Control for Skid-Steer Loaders

sections.text:
Optimizing robot poses and the map simultaneously has been shown to provide more accurate SLAM results. However, for non-feature based SLAM approaches, directly optimizing all the robot poses and the whole map will greatly increase the computational cost, making SLAM problems difficult to solve in large-scale environments.

To solve the 2D non-feature based SLAM problem in large-scale environments more accurately and efficiently, we propose the grid-based submap joining method. Specifically, we first formulate the 2D grid-based submap joining problem as a non-linear least squares (NLLS) form to optimize the global occupancy map and local submap frames simultaneously.

We then prove that in solving the NLLS problem using Gauss-Newton (GN) method, the increments of the poses in each iteration are independent of the occupancy values of the global occupancy map. Based on this property, we propose a poseonly GN algorithm equivalent to full GN method to solve the NLLS problem.

The proposed submap joining algorithm is very efficient due to the independent property and the pose-only solution.

Evaluations using simulations and publicly available practical 2D laser datasets confirm the outperformance of our proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency and accuracy, as well as the ability to solve the grid-based SLAM problem in very large-scale environments.

summary.en: The paper proposes grid-based submap joining for large-scale 2D non-feature-based SLAM, jointly optimizing a global occupancy map and local submap frames. The authors formulate the problem as nonlinear least squares and show that Gauss–Newton pose increments are independent of global map occupancy values. They use this property to derive a pose-only algorithm equivalent to full Gauss–Newton. Simulations and evaluations on public 2D laser datasets are reported to show improved efficiency and accuracy over the compared methods and support very large-scale mapping.
summary.zh: 本文针对大规模环境中的二维非特征式SLAM，提出网格子地图拼接方法，同时优化全局占据栅格地图和局部子地图坐标系。作者将问题表示为非线性最小二乘，并证明高斯—牛顿迭代中的位姿增量独立于全局地图的占据值，据此提出等价于完整高斯—牛顿方法的仅位姿算法。仿真和公开二维激光数据集评估显示，该方法在效率和精度方面优于所比较的现有方法，并可处理超大规模网格SLAM问题。

items.title: Grid-based Submap Joining: An Efficient Algorithm for Simultaneously Optimizing Global Occupancy Map and Local Submap Frames

sections.text:
Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning.

We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback.

Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles.

To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss.

The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data.

In simulation, it improves $\pi_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

summary.en: Agentic-Teacher is an autonomous data engine that uses failures of a vision-language-action model to generate and curate post-training demonstrations. Given a checkpoint, task specification, and environment tools, it analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies generate successful continuations from difficult states. The method adds temporally correlated action noise, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories with the frozen base model’s flow-matching loss. In simulation, it improves π₀ success rates on LIBERO-10, MetaWorld-10, and three RoboCasa tasks.
summary.zh: 本文提出Agentic-Teacher，用于依据视觉—语言—动作模型的失败情况生成并筛选后训练示范。给定模型检查点、任务说明和环境工具后，系统分析失败轨迹、选择干预状态，并通过执行反馈迭代开发闭环代码策略；验证后的策略生成模型难以完成状态的成功后续轨迹。系统还加入时间相关动作噪声、去除空闲帧并保留夹爪转换，再用冻结基础模型的流匹配损失筛选轨迹。仿真中，该方法提升了π₀在LIBERO-10、MetaWorld-10及三项RoboCasa任务上的成功率。

items.title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training

sections.text:
Personalized bioelectronic devices for wound therapy require not only conformal fabrication on complex body surfaces but also functional adaptation of their electrical characteristics to individual wound geometries.

Here, we present an AI-guided robotic in situ printing platform for fabricating wireless wound electrotherapy devices directly on transparent wound dressings. The system integrates a 3D vision camera, a six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, direct-ink-writing, and geometry-aware RF design optimization.

AI-based wound segmentation is used to determine wound dimensions and local surface curvature, while the reconstructed three-dimensional geometry is incorporated into the electromagnetic design of the receiving coil and interdigitated electrodes.

In contrast to conventional approaches that use surface geometry only for trajectory generation, the proposed method accounts for both anatomical curvature and tissue dielectric loading to compensate for geometry-induced shifts in resonant behavior.

A printable silver ink was characterized in terms of rheology, dimensional reproducibility, electrical resistance, and electromechanical stability, and was used to fabricate multilayer wireless devices directly on curved polyurethane dressings.

Wireless power transfer, impedance characteristics, and electric-field delivery were evaluated experimentally and numerically.

Finally, robotic in situ fabrication was demonstrated on an anthropomorphic tissue-equivalent forearm phantom, where the measured dielectric properties of the phantom were incorporated into the RF optimization, enabling resonant operation near the target frequency of 25 MHz.

This work establishes a perception-to-design-to-fabrication framework for geometry-adaptive wireless bioelectronics and provides a technological foundation for future physical-AI-enabled manufacturing of personalized on-body electrotherapy devices.

summary.en: The paper presents an AI-guided robotic platform that prints wireless wound electrotherapy devices directly onto transparent dressings. Vision-based segmentation estimates wound dimensions and curvature, which, together with tissue dielectric loading, informs RF design of the receiving coil and electrodes to address geometry-induced resonance shifts. The authors characterize printable silver ink and fabricate multilayer devices on curved dressings, evaluating power transfer, impedance, and electric-field delivery experimentally and numerically. Robotic fabrication is also demonstrated on a tissue-equivalent forearm phantom, with measured dielectric properties incorporated into optimization for resonance near the 25 MHz target.
summary.zh: 本文提出一种 AI 引导的机器人原位打印平台，可在透明伤口敷料上制造无线伤口电疗器件。系统通过视觉分割获取伤口尺寸和曲率，并将三维几何及组织介电负载纳入接收线圈与电极的射频设计，以补偿共振偏移。作者表征银墨水并在弯曲敷料上制备多层器件，结合实验和数值方法评估无线供电、阻抗与电场传递。研究还在组织等效前臂模型上演示机器人制造，测量介电性质用于优化，器件在接近目标频率25 MHz处实现共振。

sections.text:
Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments.

However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions.

In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances.

Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs.

We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains.

Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.

summary.en: The paper introduces PROOF, a locomotion framework designed to maintain robustness when legged robots encounter degraded vision, including occlusion and illumination changes. Its two-stage teacher-student approach models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven behavior and proprioceptive fallbacks, while the student predicts uncertain exteroceptive features and suppresses them for out-of-distribution inputs. In real-world evaluations on a Unitree Go2 with a depth camera, the robot performed dynamic parkour over gaps, platforms, and narrow beams under normal vision, and maintained stable locomotion under severe visual degradation.
summary.zh: 本文提出 PROOF，一种面向腿式机器人的感知鲁棒运动框架，针对遮挡、反光和光照变化等视觉退化情况，采用教师—学生两阶段学习来建模感知可靠性。教师学习依赖感知的行为及本体感觉回退行为；学生预测带不确定性的外感知特征，并在分布外输入下抑制这些特征。作者在配备深度相机的 Unitree Go2 四足机器人上开展真实环境评估：正常视觉条件下完成跨越间隙、平台和窄梁的高动态动作；严重遮挡或强光照变化时仍保持稳定运动。

sections.text:
The rapid emergence of foundation models, particularly large language models and vision-language models, has introduced a transformative paradigm in robotics.

The models offer powerful capabilities in semantic understanding, high-level reasoning, and cross-modal generalization, enabling significant advances in perception, planning, control, and human-robot interaction.

This critical review provides a structured synthesis of recent developments and organizes applications into four directions: simulation-driven robotics, open-world operation, sim-to-real transfer, and adaptable robotic systems.

Unlike existing surveys that emphasize isolated capabilities, this work highlights integrated, system-level strategies and evaluates their practical feasibility in real-world environments.

Key enabling trends such as procedural scene generation, policy generalization, and multimodal reasoning are discussed alongside core bottlenecks, including limited embodiment, lack of multimodal data, safety risks, and computational constraints.

Through this lens, this paper identifies both the architectural strengths and critical limitations of foundation model-based robotics, highlighting open challenges in real-time operation, grounding, resilience, and trust.

The review concludes with a roadmap of proposed future research directions for bridging semantic reasoning and physical intelligence through more robust, interpretable, and embodied models.

summary.en: This review surveys foundation models, especially large language and vision-language models, in robotics. It organizes applications into simulation-driven robotics, open-world operation, sim-to-real transfer, and adaptable robotic systems, emphasizing integrated strategies and their practical feasibility. The authors discuss trends such as procedural scene generation, policy generalization, and multimodal reasoning, alongside limitations including restricted embodiment, insufficient multimodal data, safety risks, and computational constraints. The review identifies challenges in real-time operation, grounding, resilience, and trust, and proposes future research directions for connecting semantic reasoning with physical intelligence.
summary.zh: 这篇综述梳理基础模型，尤其是大语言模型和视觉语言模型在机器人领域的进展，并按仿真驱动机器人、开放世界运行、仿真到现实迁移和可适应机器人四个方向组织应用。作者强调系统层面的整合策略及其现实可行性，讨论程序化场景生成、策略泛化和多模态推理等趋势，也指出具身能力有限、多模态数据不足、安全风险和算力约束等瓶颈。综述进一步归纳实时运行、落地、韧性与可信度方面的挑战，并提出未来研究路线，以连接语义推理与物理智能。

items.title: Foundation Model Driven Robotics: A Comprehensive Review

sections.text:
AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings.

This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots.

Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements.

Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows.

We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

summary.en: This structured scoping review examines the shift from AI-enabled remote patient monitoring toward agentic systems and robotics in care. It finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: most systems remain human-led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI are largely at the prototype or pilot stage. Healthcare robots can turn AI recommendations into speech, movement, prompts, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination. The authors argue that progress requires safe, interoperable architectures and auditable workflows that support interruption, clinical accountability, human oversight, and explicit AI governance.
summary.zh: 这篇结构化范围综述考察 AI 远程患者监测向代理式系统和机器人发展的趋势。作者认为成熟的代理式照护尚未出现，多数系统仍由人主导，较强的决策与行动耦合及具身 AI 主要处于原型或试点阶段。医疗机器人使监测转向行动的过程更为明显，可将 AI 建议转化为语音、移动、提醒、身体协助、升级处理和照护协调，因此具身能力、临床整合、人类监督与治理都是设计要求。作者提出，未来应建立安全、互操作且可审计、可中断并受人工监督的照护工作流。

sections.text:
Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously.

We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots.

Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance.

On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control.

The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route.

During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

summary.en: The report presents X-Nav, a system for long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation on a humanoid robot. Its MELIOR model uses only onboard RGB images and either predicts actions or a navigation goal; X-Navarch breaks brief instructions into subtasks and deploys navigation with obstacle avoidance. On a Lingxi X2, the system completed an approximately hundred-metre mission from an office lobby to a store in a neighboring building, using LiDAR and odometry for target approach and low-level control. The authors also report digital-twin adaptation and competitive R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmark results.

sections.text:
State estimation techniques for continuum robots (CRs) typically involve using computationally complex dynamic models, simplistic shape approximations, or are limited to quasi-static methods. These approaches can be sensitive to unmodeled disturbances acting on the robot.

Inspired by a factor-graph optimization paradigm, this work introduces a continuous-time stochastic state estimation framework for continuum robots. We introduce factors based on continuous-time kinematics that are corrupted by a white noise Gaussian process (GP).

By using a simple robot model paired with high-rate sensing, we show adaptability to unmodeled external forces and data dropout. The result contains an estimate of the mean and covariance for the robot's pose, velocity, and strain, each of which can be interpolated continuously in both space and time.

This same interpolation scheme can be used during estimation, allowing for inclusion of measurements that are asynchronous to the estimated states. Our method's inherent sparsity leads to a linear solve complexity with respect to time and interpolation queries in constant time.

We demonstrate our method on a CR with gyroscope and pose sensors, highlighting its versatility in real-world systems.

summary.en: The paper introduces a continuous-time stochastic state-estimation framework for continuum robots, inspired by factor-graph optimization. It uses continuous-time kinematic factors corrupted by a white-noise Gaussian process, together with a simple robot model and high-rate sensing. The authors report adaptability to unmodeled external forces and data dropout, and continuous estimates of the mean and covariance of pose, velocity, and strain. The estimates support interpolation in space and time and inclusion of asynchronous measurements. A robot with gyroscope and pose sensors is used for a real-world demonstration.
summary.zh: 本文提出一种连续时间随机状态估计框架，用于连续体机器人。方法受因子图优化启发，基于受白噪声高斯过程扰动的连续时间运动学因子，结合简化机器人模型与高速传感。作者报告，该方法可适应未建模外力和数据缺失，并连续估计机器人位姿、速度与应变的均值和协方差，支持时空插值及异步测量纳入估计。其稀疏性使求解复杂度随时间线性增长，插值查询为常数时间。研究以配备陀螺仪和位姿传感器的机器人展示了方法。

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for.

Adapting them to a new experiment still requires extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal.

SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together.

We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

sections.text:
Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings.

However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests.

In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas.

Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important.

To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning.

Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems.

We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.

items.title: Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to execute experiments autonomously. Biology and chemistry have adopted these systems.

However, increasing SDL complexity heightens susceptibility to unexpected faults in automated workflows, highlighting the need for efficient recovery mechanisms. In this study, we investigate telerobotic interventions to enhance SDL resilience against unexpected failures.

We developed a teleoperation interface enabling human operators to resolve disruptions during automated tasks. The interface enables precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro).

Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode mapping all six DOFs to the 3D mouse's central knob and (ii) a decoupled mode separating translational and rotational motions. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators intervened across three SDL fault scenarios.

In the first study, comparative trials showed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion times and reduced rotational motion. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without reference-path guidance.

Users were more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but showed behavioral differences under different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery, informing teleoperation interface optimization.

This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining robotic precision with human adaptability and problem-solving. These findings also provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.

items.title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions

sections.text:
Vision-based dexterous in-hand manipulation requires knowing not only where an object is, but also how it moves.

However, most robotic manipulation systems rely on off-the-shelf visual perception models whose outputs are limited to static object masks, geometry, or 6D poses, leaving downstream controllers to infer object dynamics implicitly from noisy visual observations.

We present VOKE, a kinematics-aware perception framework that augments existing object and hand-object pose estimators to recover a complete object kinematic state comprising pose, linear and angular velocity, and linear and angular acceleration. VOKE contains two core perception modules and a downstream application study.

First, a Pluggable Kinematics Module (PKM) attaches to the output of a standard pose estimator and predicts the object's linear and angular velocity and acceleration from temporal visual features.

Second, a Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module (KPRM) converts this motion vector into a second-order, motion-prior reference pose and refines the per-frame pose estimates.

We evaluate VOKE on DexYCB and OakInk, where it consistently improves object pose estimation across three different backbones and substantially reduces velocity and acceleration estimation error compared with pose differencing.

As a downstream application, we use Kinematics-Augmented Reinforcement Learning (KARL) to compare a kinematics-augmented policy with a pose-history baseline.

After training the policies in simulation, we transfer the kinematics-augmented policy to the physical robot without policy fine-tuning, demonstrating the complete perception-to-control pathway in the target domain.

summary.en: The paper presents VOKE, which estimates object pose, linear and angular velocity, and acceleration from temporal visual features. Its Pluggable Kinematics Module predicts motion, while a motion-guided refinement module uses that vector to improve frame-level pose estimates. The authors report improved pose estimation across three backbones and lower velocity and acceleration errors on DexYCB and OakInk. In a downstream study, KARL policies are trained in simulation; the kinematics-augmented policy is transferred to a physical robot without policy fine-tuning, demonstrating a perception-to-control pathway.

sections.text:
World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations.

Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts.

Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction.

We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives.

LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls.

Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations.

We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

summary.en: The paper introduces LASR, an offline metric for measuring whether world-model latents support action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. GeoLASR summarizes typical support, while WorstLASR captures the weakest case. The benchmark uses recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes, episode-held-out splits, a common predictor, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel reportedly show that LASR detects action information, rejects representative shortcuts, and compares imperfect latents. It is also used to train and audit a residual adapter; its better point estimates are described as such, with uncertainty assessed through paired comparisons.

items.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models

sections.text:
Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior.

The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action.

ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface.

The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff.

The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code.

On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

summary.en: The paper presents ESI, which uses environmental interaction to iteratively refine prompts, a shared skill interface, and VLA parameters, then redeploys the modular components together. LLM subtask decisions provide semantic supervision; effective corrections and subsequent student actions supervise recovery and handoff. The student also learns from useful local execution even when an episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, the authors report a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41%, without generating task-specific control code. They report outperforming the listed hybrid embodied-agent reference results and compared code-based methods on both metrics.

items.title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents

sections.text:
Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination.

At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control.

The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements.

In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance.

In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.

summary.en: The paper presents PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for humanoid table tennis doubles, where teammates must alternate strikes while sharing a confined space. A team planner selects positioning targets and filters risky proposals using learned risk estimates, while individual footwork and striking skills support movement and racket control. Human motion references guide training, and a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements supplies feedback for refining strikes. In simulation, the framework improves return success by 13.2% over a baseline, with about 2 cm positioning error. Real-world experiments report a 2.4-second, 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle and more than 10 alternating strikes by two robots.

sections.text:
Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation.

We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided.

Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field.

We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io

summary.en: The paper presents a framework that uses a vision-language model to infer safety constraints for robot manipulation from the task and scene. Given an RGB-D observation and natural-language instruction, the system first decides whether to reject a task that could lead to an unrecoverable hazard. Otherwise, it identifies preventable hazards between object pairs and specifies spatial relations to avoid. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth ground the objects in 3D, where continuous risk fields represent hazardous regions. An obstacle-avoidance module uses these fields to correct nominal robot motions during execution. The authors evaluate preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real world; the abstract reports no quantitative results.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种利用视觉语言模型推断任务及场景相关安全约束的机器人操作框架。系统根据 RGB-D 观察和自然语言任务指令，先判断任务是否可能导致不可恢复的危险，必要时拒绝执行；否则识别可预防的物体对危险，并指定需要避开的空间关系。随后，开放词汇分割和深度信息将相关物体定位到三维空间，构建连续风险场表示危险区域。执行时，避障模块结合风险场修正机器人原定动作。作者在仿真和真实环境中评估了可预防危险、需拒绝任务及其安全变体，但摘要未给出定量结果。

sections.text:
Experience from past tasks can help embodied agents perform new tasks, but it may not remain applicable or effective when conditions change. Tasks with different overall goals often share subgoals, providing a basis for cross-task experience transfer.

We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing outcome-grounded subgoal experiences and composing them in new tasks. Each experience describes how to pursue a subgoal, when the guidance applies, and what outcome must be verified for completion.

Verified outcomes from applying one experience can satisfy the conditions for applying another, allowing experiences from different past tasks to be composed online.

By examining the actions and observed outcomes at the subgoal level, EmbodiExp retains experience from successful subgoals and uses explicit action failures to identify actions to avoid under specific conditions. Experiments on EmbodiedBench and VIGIL assess cross-task transfer with experiences kept fixed throughout held-out evaluation.

EmbodiExp achieves success rates of 68.0% on EB-Habitat and 68.3% on EB-ALFRED, compared with 50.0% and 54.7% for the agent without stored experience.

summary.en: The paper presents EmbodiExp, a framework for building outcome-grounded subgoal experiences and composing experiences from past tasks in new tasks. Each experience states how to pursue a subgoal, when its guidance applies, and what outcome must be verified. A verified outcome can satisfy the conditions for another experience, enabling online composition. The framework retains successful subgoal experiences and uses explicit action failures to identify actions to avoid under particular conditions. Experiments on EmbodiedBench and VIGIL assess cross-task transfer with experiences fixed during held-out evaluation. EmbodiExp reports success rates of 68.0% on EB-Habitat and 68.3% on EB-ALFRED, versus 50.0% and 54.7% for an agent without stored experience.
summary.zh: 论文提出 EmbodiExp，用于构建以结果为依据的子目标经验，并将不同过往任务中的经验组合到新任务中。每条经验描述如何追求子目标、何时适用，以及完成时须验证的结果；一条经验所验证的结果也可满足另一条经验的适用条件，从而支持在线组合。框架分析子目标层面的动作和观察结果，保留成功经验，并依据明确的动作失败识别特定条件下应避免的动作。作者在 EmbodiedBench 和 VIGIL 上评估跨任务迁移，评估期间固定经验；EB-Habitat 和 EB-ALFRED 成功率分别为68.0%和68.3%，无存储经验的智能体分别为50.0%和54.7%。

The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks.

Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy.

Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics.

Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences.

Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy.

sections.text:
Safe navigation of robot collectives requires coordinating motion and deformation so that the collective can traverse constrained environments while ensuring each robot's safety.

Existing controllers for swarmalator collectives largely rely on local control, where each robot receives an individual command, which causes the control and communication requirements to grow with the number of agents.

We introduce a broadcast control formulation in which a single spatially affine field governs both the motion and deformation of the collective. The scalar component of the field regulates collective size, and its spatial gradient generates collective translation through non-reciprocal interactions.

Both components enter the collective dynamics directly, which allows per-robot wall, actuation, and cohesion constraints to be enforced using control barrier functions within a single quadratic program for the whole collective.

The resulting controller continuously adapts the collective size to the local environment, and enables safe passage through corridors narrower than the unconstrained collective without pre-planned resizing.

We further derive how the available actuation budget determines the reachable speed and minimum passable corridor width, and we demonstrate that two independently driven collectives can simultaneously traverse a shared junction using distinct fixed phase labels without inter-collective coordination.

summary.en: The paper introduces broadcast control for robot collectives using one spatially affine field to govern motion and deformation. Its scalar component regulates collective size, while its spatial gradient produces translation through non-reciprocal interactions. Control barrier functions enforce per-robot wall, actuation, and cohesion constraints in one quadratic program. The controller adapts collective size to the environment, enabling passage through narrower corridors without planned resizing. The authors derive relationships between actuation budget, reachable speed, and minimum corridor width, and demonstrate two independently driven collectives traversing a shared junction using distinct fixed phase labels.

sections.text:
Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is.

A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$.

Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise.

The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them.

Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well.

Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

sections.text:
Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6\,\% of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits.

On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy.

The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed.

Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes.

This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes.

Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations.

Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware.

Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($\pi_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA.

We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

sections.text:
Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content.

To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions.

The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA).

We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination.

Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88).

We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot.

These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach.

We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts.

No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze.

On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%.The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.
